5126.etyen:
Borrowed from Middle Low German bekomen (“to come to something; to get; to come into a certain state”), from Old Saxon bikuman (“to come to, arrive at”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bikwemaną (“to come to, arrive”). By surface analysis, be- (“prefix”) + komme (“to come”).
The original sense was “to come to something”, later developing into “to get, receive” and “to come into a certain state”; the Norwegian sense “to agree with, suit, have an effect on” is especially preserved in phrases such as vel bekomme (“may it do you good; you are welcome”).
Compare Danish bekomme, Swedish bekomma, Ge

6.etyen:
First attested in 1869. Unadapted borrowing from French à (“to, in, on, at”), from Old French a (“to, towards, belonging to”), ultimately from Latin ad (“to, towards, at”), from Proto-Italic *ad (“toward, to, at”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“near, at”). 12550.etyen:
Compound of e (“E”) + moll (“minor”), literally “E minor”.
The first element e (“E”) is the name of the musical note E. The second element moll (“minor”) is via German Moll (“minor”) from Middle High German bēmolle (“B-flat; soft B”), from Medieval Latin b molle (“soft B”). The adjective is from Latin mollis (“soft, mild”), from Proto-Italic *moldus (“soft”), from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥dús (“soft, weak”), from the root *(s)meld- (“to soften, melt”).
Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk e-moll, Swedish e-moll, Danish e-mol, German e-Moll and Finnish e-molli (“E minor”).

en.g: a female given name from Old Norse

1005062.etyen:
Attested in Norway from around 1875. A Danish-influenced variant of Bothild, with Bod- replacing Bot-; alternatively, the form may have arisen under direct influence from Danish Bodil. Both routes ultimately continue Old Norse Bóthildr.
The Old Norse name is formed from bót (“remedy, help, improvement”) and hildr (“battle, fight”), literally “remedy-battle”. The first element, bót (“remedy, help, improvement”), is from Proto-Germanic *bōtō (“improvement, betterment; recompense, atonement”), while the second element, hildr (“battle, fight”), is from Proto-Germanic *hildiz (“battle, fight”).
